trump-saudi-nuclear-israel-condition.headline: Trump ties Saudi nuclear deal to Israel recognition
trump-saudi-nuclear-israel-condition.body_md:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman shook hands in Riyadh on Wednesday over a signed agreement: a civil nuclear cooperation pact, the kind of long-gestating infrastructure deal that typically takes years to negotiate and decades to pay off. Washington would back a Saudi civilian nuclear power program, giving American firms priority access to supply reactors and fuel for a partnership expected to be worth billions of dollars over its lifetime. Saudi Arabia would not be permitted to enrich uranium on its own soil — a red line the US has held since talks began.

By Thursday, President Trump had added a condition nobody in Riyadh remembers agreeing to.

"Will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords," Trump wrote on Truth Social, tying the nuclear pact to Saudi normalization of relations with Israel. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt confirmed the stakes bluntly: without accession to the Accords, in her words, the nuclear "deal is off."

![Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whose government has said a Palestinian statehood pathway remains a precondition for normalizing relations with Israel.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9a/%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B5%D9%88%D8%B1%D8%A9_%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B1%D8%B3%D9%85%D9%8A%D8%A9_%D9%84%D9%84%D8%A3%D9%85%D9%8A%D8%B1_%D9%85%D8%AD%D9%85%D8%AF_%D8%A8%D9%86_%D8%B3%D9%84%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%86_%D8%A8%D9%86_%D8%B9%D8%A8%D8%AF%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B9%D8%B2%D9%8A%D8%B2_%D8%A2%D9%84_%D8%B3%D8%B9%D9%88%D8%AF.jpg)

## A day of daylight between the signature and the price tag

The sequencing matters. Had the condition been part of the original announcement, it would have been unremarkable — a known Trump preference for bundling deals, disclosed up front. Instead, the administration presented the nuclear pact on Wednesday as a freestanding energy and technology agreement, the kind of deliverable that gets read as evidence Washington and Riyadh are deepening ties independent of the Israel question. Then, less than 24 hours later, Trump reframed it as leverage.

A Saudi official's response, relayed to reporters, was terse: "It was signed. So nothing to renegotiate. Tweets don't overturn signed agreements." That is a defensible legal position — the text goes to Congress for review regardless, and a social media post does not amend a signed intergovernmental accord. But it also captures the credibility problem the reversal creates. If a headline deal can be re-priced by presidential post the morning after signing, every other agreement bearing Trump's signature invites the same question: is this final, or provisional pending whatever gets attached to it next.

## Why Riyadh isn't expected to fold

Saudi Arabia's position on Israel has been consistent for years and hasn't moved: Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has said repeatedly that normalization requires a credible pathway to Palestinian statehood, not just a ceremony. That is politically load-bearing for Riyadh in a way it wasn't for the UAE, Bahrain or Morocco, which signed the original Abraham Accords in 2020 without extracting comparable commitments on the Palestinian question. Saudi Arabia, as custodian of Islam's two holiest sites and the Arab world's largest economy, has more domestic and pan-Arab political exposure than any of those three — and less to gain from moving fast.

The optics have also shifted since October 2023. The kingdom has spent the past two years positioning itself as a steady hand in a region racked by the [Gaza war's aftermath and now the widening confrontation with Iran](iran-war-widens) — not as a supplicant likely to fold under a nuclear-deal deadline. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, for his part, welcomed Trump's framing without hesitation, calling Saudi accession to the Accords a potential "historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East. Peace through Strength." That eagerness on Israel's side only sharpens the contrast with Riyadh's silence — MBS has not been reported in contact with the White House since the condition was announced.

![Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who called Saudi accession to the Abraham Accords a potential "historic leap forward" after Trump's announcement.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e5/MOU_signing_with_Secretary_Burgum%2C_Secretary_Wright%2C_and_Israeli_PM_Benjamin_Netanyahu_on_July_8%2C_2025_-_8.jpg)

## What's actually at stake beyond the headline

The nuclear agreement itself is a genuine strategic prize for Washington, not a minor sweetener. A so-called "123 agreement" under the US Atomic Energy Act, paired with a bilateral safeguards accord, locks American firms in as the preferred suppliers for a nuclear buildout that Saudi Arabia has signaled it will pursue with or without the United States — China and Russia have both courted Riyadh's civilian nuclear business in recent years, without insisting on the enrichment ban Washington has secured. Losing the deal to a Saudi walkout wouldn't just cost American contractors billions in reactor and fuel contracts; it would hand Beijing or Moscow a foothold in a program with obvious dual-use sensitivities in a region where Iran's own nuclear ambitions remain the reason enrichment limits exist at all.

That is the tension Trump has now introduced into his own leverage play. The Abraham Accords condition assumes Saudi Arabia wants the nuclear deal badly enough to move on Israel. But if Riyadh calculates that Washington wants the nuclear deal — and the strategic foothold that comes with it — just as badly, the condition could backfire, pushing Saudi Arabia toward alternative suppliers rather than toward Jerusalem. Congress, which must still review the agreement's text once released, adds a further layer of uncertainty: lawmakers uneasy about proliferation risk in the region could complicate ratification independent of anything Trump says about Israel.

## What to watch

The agreement's full text has not yet been made public and is due to be transmitted to Congress for review — that filing, whenever it lands, will show whether the enrichment prohibition and any Israel-related language are actually written into the deal or remain confined to Trump's public statements. Riyadh's near-term response, or lack of one, will signal whether the kingdom treats the ultimatum as a real deadline or something to wait out. And with Gulf diplomacy already strained by the Iran war's expansion, any Saudi move — toward Washington's terms or away from them — will be read across the region as a signal of where Gulf states are willing to plant their flags next.

gsk-jideytro-fda-approval.headline: GSK wins FDA approval for Jideytro
gsk-jideytro-fda-approval.body_md:
GSK has picked up its first-ever US approval for a lung cancer drug, and the timing is no accident. The Food and Drug Administration cleared Jideytro (zidesamtinib) on Thursday for adults with locally advanced or metastatic ROS1-positive non-small cell lung cancer who have already tried and failed a prior ROS1 inhibitor — a decision that landed nearly two months ahead of its scheduled September 18 target date.[^1]

The drug is not homegrown. It arrived via GSK's $10.6 billion acquisition of Nuvalent, a Massachusetts biotech, which closed on July 15 — just over a week before the approval.[^2] For a company that spent that sum acquiring a single-asset oncology pipeline, a rapid green light is the best possible first data point, though it does not by itself tell shareholders whether the deal will pay for itself.

![GSK's former Brentford, London headquarters](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/86/Brentford.Boston_Manor_Park.Glaxo_Smith_Kline_building.20190224_170442.jpg)

## What the drug does

ROS1-positive NSCLC is a genetically distinct, uncommon form of lung cancer — researchers estimate roughly 50,000 new cases diagnosed worldwide each year, concentrated among non-smokers in their 40s and 50s.[^3] Jideytro is designed as a next-generation, ROS1-selective inhibitor for patients whose disease has progressed after an earlier ROS1 drug, with claimed advantages in target selectivity, coverage of resistance mutations, and the ability to cross the blood-brain barrier — relevant because ROS1-positive tumours frequently spread to the brain.[^1]

The approval rests on the ARROS-1 Phase I/II trial, a single-arm study of 117 previously treated patients. The objective response rate was 44% (95% confidence interval: 34–53%), with 82% of responders still responding at six months and 69% at twelve.[^1] Those are respectable but not exceptional numbers for a second-line therapy in a small, well-defined patient population — the kind of drug that matters enormously to the people who have it, without moving GSK's overall revenue base by much on its own.

"The rapid progression of Jideytro from development to approval reflects both the strength of the underlying science and the urgent need for additional effective and tolerable treatments for ROS1-positive lung cancer," said Tony Wood, GSK's chief scientific officer, in the company's statement.[^2]

## A crowded, narrow market

Jideytro is not entering an empty field. Pfizer's Xalkori and Bristol Myers Squibb's Augtyro already treat ROS1-positive disease, and Nuvation Bio's Ibtrozi (taletrectinib) — approved by the FDA in June 2025 — reported $18.5 million in first-quarter 2026 sales, giving a rough sense of scale for this niche.[^4] None of the reporting so far on Jideytro discloses a US list price, expected peak sales, or how GSK intends to position it against those rivals, which is precisely the gap that limits its use as an investment signal today.

What the approval does confirm is that GSK's oncology pipeline is now genuinely multi-drug. Jideytro joins a portfolio anchored by the meningitis B vaccine Bexsero and the cancer immunotherapy Jemperli, and GSK has more assets queued behind it from the same Nuvalent deal — including neladalkib, an ALK inhibitor with an FDA decision expected November 27, and an early-stage HER2-altered NSCLC candidate.[^4] Regulatory momentum across a pipeline is usually a stronger valuation signal than any single approval, and this is the second data point in that thesis inside two weeks.

## What's missing for investors

GSK shares have not shown a clear reaction to the news, and the company's pharmaceutical announcements have not reliably moved the stock in either direction recently. The most recent analyst rating on GSK carries a Sell recommendation with a price target of £19.00, a reminder that pipeline wins alone rarely settle an equity story.[^5] Until GSK or analysts publish pricing, reimbursement, and peak-sales estimates for Jideytro, the approval reads as a scientific and regulatory milestone rather than a quantifiable input to the company's valuation.

The next marker to watch is neladalkib's FDA decision in late November — a second, larger test of whether the Nuvalent acquisition is compounding value beyond its purchase price, and the first point at which analysts are likely to attach real numbers to GSK's new lung cancer franchise.

doj-drops-nyt-subpoenas.headline: DOJ drops subpoenas against NYT reporters in leak probe
doj-drops-nyt-subpoenas.body_md:
The Justice Department has backed away from one of the more aggressive press subpoenas in recent memory, telling a federal judge Thursday it would withdraw grand jury subpoenas against New York Times reporters over their coverage of security gaps in President Trump's new, Qatari-donated Air Force One.

The retreat came at the end of a hearing in the Southern District of New York, where U.S. District Judge Arun Subramanian had made plain that the subpoenas would either be withdrawn voluntarily or quashed by the court. Facing that choice, a DOJ lawyer, Sean Buckley, conceded the department had made errors. "That was an error, judge, which we own," he told Subramanian. "It was a consequence of trying to move quickly." The judge was unmoved by the framing: subpoenas to journalists, he reminded the room, citing the department's own regulations, "are the last step, not the first step, but the last step."

![The New York Times Building in Manhattan](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a9/The_New_York_Times_Building_at_sunset%2C_2021-09-30.jpg)

The case began in early July, after the Times published reporting — bylined by Julian E. Barnes, Eric Lipton, Tyler Pager and Eric Schmitt — on why Trump used the old Air Force One rather than the new Boeing 747-8 gifted by Qatar to leave a NATO summit in Turkey, and on the newer jet's thinner security features, including its lack of the anti-missile systems fitted to the aircraft it is meant to replace. Days later, federal agents showed up at reporters' homes to serve subpoenas demanding grand jury testimony about who had leaked the details. The requests went further than the bylines: prosecutors also sought phone records for two reporters' spouses and for one reporter's mother, a mental-health professional with confidentiality obligations to her own clients, and asked for records stretching back to January 1 — months before the articles that supposedly triggered the investigation.

## Last resort, not first

That mismatch between the leak under investigation and the sweep of the subpoenas became the case's central problem. Longstanding Justice Department policy treats compelling journalists' testimony or records as a measure of last resort, used only once other investigative avenues are exhausted — a norm meant to keep leak inquiries from turning into fishing expeditions through newsrooms. Bruce D. Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, said the subpoenas "break from longstanding Justice Department practice to protect the public interest and press independence," calling the home visits from federal agents "an extraordinary assault on the freedom of the press." David McCraw, the Times' deputy general counsel, was similarly blunt in court filings, saying the sight of law enforcement on reporters' doorsteps "should shock the conscience of any American who believes in the Constitution."

With the subpoenas now void, McCraw struck a more measured note: "Today's proceeding was an important affirmation of our country's commitment to a free press." The department, for its part, is not conceding the underlying fight — a spokesperson said the investigation "remains ongoing" and that it would continue to "pursue justice against those threatening national security by leaking classified information," while also complaining that Subramanian had blocked prosecutors from laying out their case.

That tension is the story to watch. Nothing stops the department from opening a narrower, better-documented subpoena the next time a leak investigation reaches a newsroom's door — the underlying authority is untouched. What changed is the cost of getting it wrong: a judge willing to call the tactic out in open court, and a Justice Department that, faced with sanctions, chose retreat over a fight it might have lost on the merits.

burnham-pub-rates-cut.headline: Burnham unveils 20% business rates cut for English pubs
burnham-pub-rates-cut.body_md:
Andy Burnham's first act of economic policy as prime minister was not a budget, a bond announcement or a growth strategy. It was a pint.

On Thursday, less than a week after entering Downing Street, Burnham confirmed a 20% cut to business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues in England, starting next April. The government says it will benefit almost 32,000 venues and save the typical pub an estimated £1,100 over the next financial year — small beer, in cash terms, against the scale of the problems the sector says it's facing.

![Andy Burnham arrives at 10 Downing Street as prime minister](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9f/Prime_Minister_Andy_Burnham_arrives_at_10_Downing_Street_%2855406667976%29.jpg)

The £100m annual cost is being funded, Downing Street says, by trimming business rate relief currently enjoyed by vape shops and by a crackdown on online marketplace sellers who dodge VAT — a pairing that reads less like fiscal strategy than like a press release designed to avoid the words "who pays for this." Pubs and live music venues were already due a 15% discount for the 2026/27 billing year under a scheme inherited from the last government, with a real-terms freeze pencilled in for the two years after. Burnham's cut builds on top of that rather than starting from scratch.

## A narrow round

The politics of the announcement were tidier than the economics. A trip to a pub makes for better pictures on day one than a spreadsheet on public borrowing, and hospitality — battered by energy costs, wage rises and a slow bleed of closures — is an easy sector to be seen backing. But the relief pointedly excludes restaurants and hotels, and that omission has produced the loudest reaction of the week.

UK Hospitality, the trade body covering the wider sector, warned that restaurants and hotels face many of the same cost pressures and called for the support to be widened. The boss of the Leon restaurant chain went further, arguing the policy "creates a divide" by helping pubs while leaving comparable businesses to face higher bills regardless. Chris Tulloch, managing director of the pub operator Blind Tiger Inns, was blunter still about what pubs themselves are getting: not "a rescue package nor a lifeline," he said, more a case of "we were going to shoot you and now we're not... it's not making things better, it just means things won't go quite as bad quite as quickly." Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's response was shorter — "Is that it?"

## What it signals

The irony is that Burnham has previously backed the industry's own preferred fix: cutting VAT on hospitality to 10%, a change trade groups argue would do more for margins than rates relief ever could. Thursday's announcement stopped well short of that, which is the real tell. A rates cut is cheap, popular and reversible; a VAT cut is none of those things, and this government is already fielding questions from bond investors about how loose its fiscal hand is going to be. For a market watching Burnham's fiscal instincts more broadly, the pub cut reads as a signal in itself — generous with headlines, careful with the Treasury's numbers. The next test comes when the wider spending review lands and hospitality finds out whether Thursday was a down payment or the whole tab.

france-bordeaux-wildfire-evacuation.headline: France evacuates 20,000 as wildfires rage near Bordeaux
france-bordeaux-wildfire-evacuation.body_md:
The fire that emptied out a corner of France's Atlantic coast this week did not begin with lightning, or a discarded cigarette, or an arsonist's match. By the account of local officials, it began with a machine sent out to prevent exactly this kind of disaster — a brush-clearing tractor working the scrubland near the village of Saumos, in the Gironde department, that malfunctioned and threw a spark into tinder-dry pine forest.

Within three hours the fire had grown sixfold. By Thursday it had burned across more than 31 square kilometres of the Landes de Gascogne, Europe's largest man-made forest, and forced the evacuation of more than 20,000 people — residents of the town of Le Porge, campers on the Lège-Cap-Ferret peninsula, and holidaymakers pulled from eight campgrounds along one of France's most visited stretches of coast, 50 kilometres west of Bordeaux.

![A Canadair water bomber flies over a forest fire near Fontainebleau, France, on July 13, 2026 — part of the same wave of blazes that reached Gironde ten days later.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ed/2026-07-13_15-32-45_-_Fontainebleau_-_Incendie.jpg)

## A machine meant to prevent fire, suspected of starting one

Judicial police have impounded the brush-clearing tractor and opened an inquiry into whether the ignition was mechanical failure or manufacturing defect. The mayor of Le Porge has described the working theory as accidental, and the local prefect responded within a day by banning all forestry work involving combustion engines across the department — an acknowledgment that the very equipment used to reduce fire risk, by clearing the undergrowth that fuels it, had become a source of it.

That irony sits at the centre of the story. Brush-clearing is standard fire prevention in a region that lost roughly 30,000 hectares of the same forest in 2022, one of the worst fire seasons in French history. The machines used to do the clearing run on the same hot, dry ground they are meant to protect, at the same time of year the ground is most flammable — a narrow operating window that leaves little margin for mechanical failure.

## Eight hundred firefighters, three borrowed planes

About 800 firefighters, backed by hundreds of gendarmes and soldiers, have been deployed against the blaze, joined by water-bombing aircraft that closed to within 300 metres of the first homes in Lège before crews managed to hold the line. France asked the European Union for help, and Brussels sent three additional water-bombing planes — a reminder that even a country with its own dedicated Canadair fleet and civil-defence corps runs short of aerial capacity once several fires demand it simultaneously.

![A Canadair CL-215/415, the model of amphibious water bomber France's Sécurité Civile flies against forest fires.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b1/Canadair_CL-215-6B11_CL-415%2C_France_-_Securite_Civile_AN0457543.jpg)

Three houses have been scorched and a caravan destroyed, but as of Thursday no injuries had been recorded from the Gironde fire itself. The same cannot be said of the wider season: two firefighters died two days earlier when their truck was overrun by flames near Bordeaux-Mérignac airport, in a separate blaze — a grim marker for what officials are already calling one of France's deadliest fire seasons in years.

## A season running four times ahead of normal

Gironde's fire arrived amid France's third heatwave since May, with the mayor of Le Porge's own neighbouring commune reporting temperatures above 30°C and winds swinging unhelpfully to the east and northeast. Nationally, more than 41,000 hectares have burned so far in 2026 — over four times the seasonal average and already ahead of 2022's record pace, according to the EU's Copernicus monitoring service. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said plainly that climate change is pulling the fire season earlier into the calendar, a claim the data increasingly supports: peak fire risk in southwestern France used to arrive in August, not late July.

The insurance industry has started to treat this as a structural shift rather than a bad run of summers. At Munich Re's wildfire roundtable in April, chief climate scientist Tobias Grimm told attendees that wildfire is now an established natural-catastrophe peril in Europe, with its frequency, intensity and geographic spread all changing — including into regions, like the pine-forested but historically low-risk stretches of the Atlantic coast, that underwriters had not priced for. Gironde, which sits at the edge of France's largest wine-producing region by volume, illustrates the exposure: even fires that stay out of the vineyards themselves can taint grapes with smoke, and insurers covering agricultural and tourism infrastructure across the department are only beginning to model that combined risk properly.

The immediate test is containment — the fire had not been fully controlled as of Thursday evening, and forecasters see little relief in the heat before the weekend. The longer test is what the impounded tractor's inquiry finds, and whether it prompts tighter rules for mechanical fire-prevention work during red-alert conditions, or is treated as an isolated malfunction in a season that will keep generating them regardless.

floor.headline: Fast Thesis, Stale Quote
floor.body_md:
Repsol made today's call in one sharp move. The earnings beat plus $571M buyback read as concrete capital return, and the market repriced it same-day — from entry straight through take-profit on an uninterrupted grind. BA.L rode the energy lean to a tidy secondary win.

ServiceNow exposed the vulnerability. Entry hit a stale quote; by scheduled close, the anticipated reaction never showed up. Price never moved; the rest was costs. When the news digests fast and the market reprices immediately, the thesis works. When repricing stalls — caught in data lag or market indifference — there's nothing to capture. Tomorrow will test whether speed is actually the edge.
